title: Natural outbursts in hilly terrain are rising amid climate change
content_html:
Disaster struck Nepal on Wednesday after a flash flood ravaged the Himalayas and foothills. As of Thursday, at least 389 people including several foreign tourists, had died, while at least 300 Indians remained missing. Satellite imagery analysed by global agencies, including the Indian Space Research Organisation, points to a glacier collapse or ice-rock avalanche in Tibet, possibly followed by a temporary river blockage and its sudden failure. An earthquake was initially suspected, but evidence has not borne it out. While the immediate flood wave has passed, there are warnings of possible secondary flooding from debris blockages upstream. There has been extensive damage along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors, with settlements washed away and hydropower and monitoring infrastructure damaged. Nepalese authorities said 35 motorable and 45 suspension bridges and about 40 kilometres of roads had been damaged.

Given that it is the monsoon, north India and the larger Himalayan regions are under the influence of a powerful Western Disturbance. It would thus not have been unreasonable to attribute the floods to these extratropical storms that can cause clouds to collide with mountains and release enormous quantities of rain at short notice. But the ubiquity of satellites is helping establish a more complex picture, pointing to collapsing glaciers and recalling the October 2023 South Lhonak Lake disaster in Sikkim. There, an eponymous Himalayan glacier suddenly gave way, releasing millions of tonnes of water, debris and rock that pulverised Sikkim’s largest hydropower project. Subsequent analysis showed that the resulting Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) had been years in the making. The Indian Himalayas have nearly 7,500 glacial lakes and about 15,000 glaciers, some monitored through remote sensing. Yet, fully assessing their condition requires site visits, difficult because these lakes lie in inhospitable terrain while expeditions are generally feasible only from July to September. Even with satellite monitoring, accurately forecasting a glacier collapse remains exceedingly difficult — and can be counterproductive if warnings trigger panic among residents who, often because of habit or lack of alternatives, are unlikely to move out of harm’s way. Dams and hydropower projects in such terrain are often among the first casualties of these natural outbursts, which are increasing amid global warming. Beyond relief and rescue, governments must enforce construction codes, discourage settlements and large projects in known vulnerable zones, and invest in better tracking of glacier health. Such monitoring can feed long-term disaster planning into development programmes. A tragedy is frequently not the result of a conspiracy but the product of passive neglect; the latter can be addressed.

title: Is English a foreign language in India?
author: Priscilla Jebaraj
content_html:
The Supreme Court has been discussing linguistics this month while hearing challenges to the CBSE’s three-language formula, which mandates that two of the three languages must be native Indian languages, a category that does not include English. The top court had wondered whether it was correct to treat English as a “non-indigenous” language, given its long history in the country, and its role as a link language in governance and higher education. So should English be considered a foreign language in India? Apoorvanand and Ganesh Devy discuss the question in a conversation moderated by Priscilla Jebaraj.

Is English a foreign language in India?

Apoorvanand: No. It came from outside the geography that we define as India now. But it has been Indianised. We cannot now say that English is foreign to the soil because it’s being used in different forms and for different purposes by people across India. 

Ganesh Devy: Hindi and English are born of the same Indo-European language family. One part of that family came to us 3,500 years ago; that was Sanskrit and one of the descendants of Sanskrit is Hindi. Another part came through Europe 400 years ago, in the 17th century. So, they both belong to the same root language, and both of them have come to us at different times.

In fact, the only major indigenous language in India is Tamil as it does not come from outside. But for that reason, we cannot impose Tamil on all students. Similarly, we cannot impose English or Hindi. So in India, the language question cannot simply be seen in terms of which is foreign, which is indigenous.

The history of English in India includes both imperialism and the freedom movement, Macaulay and Gandhi. How has this complicated the issue?

Ganesh Devy: Macaulay’s minute is relatively recent, dated 1835; the East India Company had started using English in India almost 230 years before that. The interaction between English and other languages started in the 17th century and intensified during the 18th century. In the 19th century, the English governors in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras insisted on teaching children in native languages, that is, the regional languages. Elphinstone very clearly gave written instructions to teach children in Gujarati and Marathi in the Bombay presidency. But by 1835, the East India Company was thinking of how to bring in legislation to replace Persian, which had been kind of a national language connecting India for several centuries, and that is when Macaulay came in.

Apoorvanand: English came as a language of traders and missionaries and gradually became the language of the administration and the state, but then it also became the language of education. We see an elite being formed through English and also the formation of nationalism or nationalist ideas through English. So that’s a very complex journey. We cannot treat English as a simple imposition on Indians. Indians adopted it, domesticated it, and then used it against those who had colonised India. Then, it became a language of liberation for many communities who did not have access to education or knowledge for generations. 

English has become the language of aspiration and status. How does that impact social and political dynamics?

Ganesh Devy: The creation of an English-speaking elite has to be seen in the historical context of an earlier experience, where Sanskrit had formed an elite which brought in the varna system. The English language created an elite in India who tried to change that system and make India a modern society. Moreover, in India, in order to get a good job one often needs to migrate outside one’s State. And as soon as migration is involved, the need for English is enhanced.

Apoorvanand: English is connected with social mobility as well as geographical mobility. No other language gives you this advantage.

According to the 2011 Census, 10% of the Indian population speak English, and the numbers are only increasing. Has this resulted in the suppression of other Indian languages or has it spread multilingualism?

Apoorvanand: It would be very simplistic to make a direct cause and effect relationship, because multi-linguality is a feature of India and there are different reasons for which people use different languages at different levels. In my Delhi classroom, the students are largely from the so-called Hindi belt. But for most of them, their home or street language is actually Bhojpuri or Braj or Avadhi or Maithili. So there are many languages which live side-by-side, performing different functions.

Being a teacher of Hindi, I regret that Hindi is in fact erasing many languages, which had a very rich tradition and which are living languages such as Maithali or Braj or Avadhi or Dondari or even Adivasi languages, because the state is not investing in them. They have now become oral languages, pushed to the margins, while all attention goes to Hindi. It’s Hindi imperialism in Hindi areas; Hindi is a coloniser.

What is the impact of the rise of English as well as Hindi on other languages?

Ganesh Devy: First, let me say that the Census of India is not at all a clear mirror as far as language is concerned. For example, if a language is spoken by less than 10,000 persons, the Census says it is not a language. Then, if you look at how many individuals are studying in universities in India, the total figure at any given time in the last 10 years would be about four crore. Each one of them know English as a second language because English is the language of higher education, and yet the Census does not reflect those figures.

Hindi has been gulping other languages. In the Census itself, some 56 other languages are included as subsets of Hindi. There is a language called Pawri which is spoken by the Pawra Adivasi community, on the border of Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, who do not understand Hindi at all. Yet that is shown as a subset of Hindi. It is the same with Tamil, Kannada and Marathi. All smaller languages are being shown as subsets of larger languages and that comes from the state’s desire to have some kind of linguistic unity.

India is made of many languages and that is the fundamental truth. Just last week, in Maharashtra, rickshaw drivers and taxi drivers were on strike because there is a compulsion that they have to pass an examination in Marathi, based on grammar. Why would a taxi driver need Marathi grammar? He has functional Marathi. Indians speak a lot of functional languages. They speak English, not as the British do, but as a functional language. They speak Hindi all over India as a functional language. And I think we should never forsake the beauty of having multiple functional languages in our pocket, in our hearts, and in our brains.

But there is also a vested interest in English in India from English language publishers and English medium schools. They bat for the continuance of English partly out of commercial interest. I don’t agree with that.

Apoorvanand: On the CBSE and their stress on a three-language formula, and the insistence of policymakers that they want children to learn the mother tongue — all this is farcical because people know that all these policymakers are sending their own children to English medium schools and that English is social capital, cultural capital, and capital in real terms.

There’s also a significant amount of Indian literature written in English today, including works in translation. And of course, films and the Internet freely mix languages. How does that change the debate?

Ganesh Devy: In the 6th, 7th, and 8th centuries, many Indians produced books in Sanskrit. Then, in the 15th and 16th centuries, India was producing more books in Persian. Today, India is producing more books in English than they produce in England. But our desi languages have still survived.

So the production of books, movies, and songs in a certain language is not necessarily an indication of a profound fundamental cultural shift. There are just two small questions to be asked to anybody who is writing English fiction or non-fiction. The first is, when that person goes into any spiritual space, is their prayer also in English? The second question is, is the audience only Indian or is it a global audience? The answers to these two questions will reveal the exact significance of the shift.

By the way, the English came here and had an impact on many things. But Indian music remains Indian music. We have internalised but not replaced. So, our cultural reception of English culture has been calibrated, granular, and is not wholesale as in Australia, U.S. or in Canada where native cultures were wiped out.

Apoorvanand: I would disagree with that. For example, in my daughter’s generation or the generation after, their first love in music is through English and not “Indian music”. I don’t see any problem in that and I don’t see them as culturally uprooted. Would we say that this young generation or those bands which sing only in English are not culturally Indian? It’s a very complex concept and the whole anxiety about maintaining nativity and creating a difference between what is indigenous and what is foreign is also problematic. Therefore, I would like to argue that English has made India its home. Those who want to declare that it’s a foreign language, in fact, want to hide the fact that Hindi colonises other languages and so do Tamil and other languages, when you create these as meta languages and others as sub languages.

Listen to the conversation

Apoorvanand is a Professor in the Hindi department of the University of Delhi. Ganesh Devy is a former professor of English and the man behind the People’s Linguistic Survey of India project

title: Rajinikanth, a secret Chennai park, and a Gandhi impersonator
author: Srinivasa Ramanujam
content_html:
The best stories in journalism are not necessarily the ones that begin with a strong pitch, or take hours of research and painstaking reporting; sometimes, they are the ones that a reporter simply discovers along the way.

Recently, I challenged myself to find the place where actor Rajinikanth had shot his first film, Apoorva Raagangal, in 1975. Tamil cinema fans will remember the iconic shot of the newcomer pushing open a gate and striding into a house — almost as if announcing his arrival in filmdom.

title: Why not normalise use of AI in writing?
author: Amit  Kumar
content_html:
Why not simply normalise the use of artificial intelligence in academic or any other forms of writing? Some will call this an ethical violation, arguing that human intellect cannot be surrendered to thoughtlessness, and that people will hand the tasks to AI and then claim the outcome as their own. But have we not already crossed that bar? Taking credit from our mechanised tools.

The potatoes a chef puts into an air fryer are sold as the “chef’s special”. The shooter gets the credit or blame for pulling the trigger, not the metallurgist or the arms manufacturer. The cosmonaut is remembered as the one who landed on the moon, and not the thousands of engineers and taxpayers who indirectly made that expedition possible. In every one of such cases, we already assign authorship to the person who directs the tool, not to the tool itself, or to every component that contributed to it. Yet, when the tool is generative AI, the same logic is suddenly reversed. The individual who directs it is accused of forfeiting authorship rather than exercising it. How come it is legitimate for a professor or researcher to claim authorship, despite taking all the help from their research assistants, such as collected and digitised data, field observations, case studies and narratives? Why such dualism?

It appears that this is not even a question of why, but whose. Whose authority is being protected by that resistance and challenged, if AI writing gets the green signal? With a good research idea and access to advanced AI tools, someone who has never set foot on remotest sites such as Antarctica or the Everest can now produce research that rivals the work of those who spent years in the field. Someone who never became bilingual can now write fluently across languages. Someone who always felt short to sharpen their own prose can now have it handed to them, polished, on a plate. Whose authority does that threaten?

Parallels in history

History gives a consistent answer as every novelty that redistributes access to power is resisted, and the resistance is rarely about the novelty itself. People resisted metal tools when stone tools were displaced. They resisted motorised wheels when animal carts were phased out. They resisted paper currency when it replaced gold and silver coins. The high-born and propertied classes resisted the idea of social reformers that everyone deserves a right to education. Every novelty has been resisted, from Galileo’s heliocentrism to the visibility of a non-binary identity in contemporary societies. And each time, the resistance came because the novelty threatened an existing arrangement of power.

Now, the question arises: who, then, benefits from labelling AI writing an “ethical violation”, and who stands at a disadvantage? Much of the loudest objection comes from a milieu long accustomed to a Western (Euro-American-centric) and elitist model of knowledge production. It is this claim of legitimate scholarship, a standard by which knowledge produced anywhere in the world is deemed worthy or unworthy. And AI has quietly punctured one of that milieu’s deepest advantages — the near-monopoly of native English fluency. A non-native speaker can now go toe-to-toe with a native English writer, with AI’s help. Outside the Anglophone world, standard “proper” English has been the single biggest challenge for brilliant minds, and AI has turned that barrier into an opportunity. In other words, a genuine redistribution of linguistic capital. The West has lost a linguistic monopoly it once did not have to defend. The discomfort around AI writing under the banner of “No, AI Please” tracks that redistribution more closely, tracking any coherent theory of authorship. AI writing has emerged as a genuine de-colonial tool for post-colonial societies, pushing back against the malpractices normalised under literary neocolonialism.

I wonder how long this charade can hold, as one can notice the selective normalisation. It is entirely acceptable to let AI generate references, citations, infographics, graphs, slide decks, and let it silently correct the grammar too. But letting it touch the sentences is not acceptable. This very selective normalisation has created an entire economy of tools such as “AI Content Humanizer”, “5th-Grade Style Writer”, “No-Fluff Humanizer”, “Natural Tone Rewriter”, “Conversational Rewriter”, and dozens more to launder AI prose back into a humanised pattern. It is strange that instead of letting AI help people cross language barriers and let their ideas flow, we normalise the malpractice of hiding it. In other words, the rule is not “don’t use AI”, rather, it is “don’t get caught”. As a professor of mine once put it, if you are going to lie, lie well enough not to get caught. And if you can’t, don’t lie at all. Consider J.K. Rowling’s Platform 9¾ at London’s King’s Cross Station, a lie told with such conviction that it convinced the world of a magical place that never existed but people now travel to see.

Not plagiarism

Now, before moving on to the arguments against AI writing, one must establish that AI use is not plagiarism. Plagiarism is theft of another’s ideas and work. AI-assisted writing is neither and entirely a separate debate. The objections raised against AI writing can be located into four broad strands: that it threatens originality and the meaning of scholarly work, heavy reliance on it dulls critical intellect, it risks leaking respondents’ personal data, and that it erodes human creativity. On reflection, scholarly worth has never been simply about originality. Illogical outcomes, rubbishness, and genocidal ideologies, too, have claimed “originality” within their own internal logic. What matters is contribution with a logical solution to the problem statement without harm. As for intellect, human habits of mind take generations to change, not possible within a span of a technology cycle. If anything, AI is capable of solving in minutes what once took months of manual labour, freeing attention for much more grave problems rather than dulling it. Third, data leakage is not an inherent property of tools such as AI, but a research-design failure, as pseudonymisation and anonymisation remain the researcher’s own ethical responsibility. And lastly, AI is not Alzheimer’s for human creativity. Better tools have never suppressed creativity. They have always redirected creativity.

Now, once these arguments are set aside, what remains is not a principled position but a familiar social reflex. The one that promotes “I have suffered through this, so you should too.” It reflects in professors’ posts on LinkedIn that they won’t read a draft touched by AI. Sounds similar to one of patriarchy’s oldest tricks: the mother-in-law who insists her daughter-in-law endure what she endured, or my office clerk who advised me to pile work on a new hire, stating why should they get an easy run when we did not. Schadenfreude dressed as rigour, a bizarre satisfaction taken in someone else’s hardship. Moreover, it is not a coincidence that the loudest objections tend to belong to those who have already cleared the language-proficiency bar the rest of the world is still trying to reach.

To conclude, AI writing is a redistribution of who gets these standards, rather than the erosion of standards. The only practical choice left is whether to accept that now, or to keep resisting a novelty to be accepted at a later stage, like everyone before it. It is inevitable that it will become the new normal, and failing to see that is not caution, but a failure of foresight. In the words of historian E.H. Carr, history can only be written by those who have a sense of direction and an instinct that they are advancing towards an end goal in order to piece evidence together convincingly. And man moves within history himself and indeed progresses.

Amit Kumar is an Assistant Professor in the Institute for Development and Communication, Chandigarh

Why not simply normalise the use of artificial intelligence in academic or any other forms of writing? Some will call this an ethical violation, arguing that human intellect cannot be surrendered to thoughtlessness, and that people will hand the tasks to AI and then claim the outcome as their own. But have we not already crossed that bar? Taking credit from our mechanised tools.
The potatoes a chef puts into an air fryer are sold as the “chef’s special”. The shooter gets the credit or blame for pulling the trigger, not the metallurgist or the arms manufacturer. The cosmonaut is remembered as the one who landed on the moon, and not the thousands of engineers and taxpayers who indirectly made that expedition possible. In every one of such cases, we already assign authorship to the person who directs the tool, not to the tool itself, or to every component that contributed to it. Yet, when the tool is generative AI, the same logic is suddenly reversed. The individual who directs it is accused of forfeiting authorship rather than exercising it. How come it is legitimate for a professor or researcher to claim authorship, despite taking all the help from their research assistants, such as collected and digitised data, field observations, case studies and narratives? Why such dualism?
It appears that this is not even a question of why, but whose. Whose authority is being protected by that resistance and challenged, if AI writing gets the green signal? With a good research idea and access to advanced AI tools, someone who has never set foot on remotest sites such as Antarctica or the Everest can now produce research that rivals the work of those who spent years in the field. Someone who never became bilingual can now write fluently across languages. Someone who always felt short to sharpen their own prose can now have it handed to them, polished, on a plate. Whose authority does that threaten?
Parallels in history
History gives a consistent answer as every novelty that redistributes access to power is resisted, and the resistance is rarely about the novelty itself. People resisted metal tools when stone tools were displaced. They resisted motorised wheels when animal carts were phased out. They resisted paper currency when it replaced gold and silver coins. The high-born and propertied classes resisted the idea of social reformers that everyone deserves a right to education. Every novelty has been resisted, from Galileo’s heliocentrism to the visibility of a non-binary identity in contemporary societies. And each time, the resistance came because the novelty threatened an existing arrangement of power.
Now, the question arises: who, then, benefits from labelling AI writing an “ethical violation”, and who stands at a disadvantage? Much of the loudest objection comes from a milieu long accustomed to a Western (Euro-American-centric) and elitist model of knowledge production. It is this claim of legitimate scholarship, a standard by which knowledge produced anywhere in the world is deemed worthy or unworthy. And AI has quietly punctured one of that milieu’s deepest advantages — the near-monopoly of native English fluency. A non-native speaker can now go toe-to-toe with a native English writer, with AI’s help. Outside the Anglophone world, standard “proper” English has been the single biggest challenge for brilliant minds, and AI has turned that barrier into an opportunity. In other words, a genuine redistribution of linguistic capital. The West has lost a linguistic monopoly it once did not have to defend. The discomfort around AI writing under the banner of “No, AI Please” tracks that redistribution more closely, tracking any coherent theory of authorship. AI writing has emerged as a genuine de-colonial tool for post-colonial societies, pushing back against the malpractices normalised under literary neocolonialism.
I wonder how long this charade can hold, as one can notice the selective normalisation. It is entirely acceptable to let AI generate references, citations, infographics, graphs, slide decks, and let it silently correct the grammar too. But letting it touch the sentences is not acceptable. This very selective normalisation has created an entire economy of tools such as “AI Content Humanizer”, “5th-Grade Style Writer”, “No-Fluff Humanizer”, “Natural Tone Rewriter”, “Conversational Rewriter”, and dozens more to launder AI prose back into a humanised pattern. It is strange that instead of letting AI help people cross language barriers and let their ideas flow, we normalise the malpractice of hiding it. In other words, the rule is not “don’t use AI”, rather, it is “don’t get caught”. As a professor of mine once put it, if you are going to lie, lie well enough not to get caught. And if you can’t, don’t lie at all. Consider J.K. Rowling’s Platform 9¾ at London’s King’s Cross Station, a lie told with such conviction that it convinced the world of a magical place that never existed but people now travel to see.
Not plagiarism
Now, before moving on to the arguments against AI writing, one must establish that AI use is not plagiarism. Plagiarism is theft of another’s ideas and work. AI-assisted writing is neither and entirely a separate debate. The objections raised against AI writing can be located into four broad strands: that it threatens originality and the meaning of scholarly work, heavy reliance on it dulls critical intellect, it risks leaking respondents’ personal data, and that it erodes human creativity. On reflection, scholarly worth has never been simply about originality. Illogical outcomes, rubbishness, and genocidal ideologies, too, have claimed “originality” within their own internal logic. What matters is contribution with a logical solution to the problem statement without harm. As for intellect, human habits of mind take generations to change, not possible within a span of a technology cycle. If anything, AI is capable of solving in minutes what once took months of manual labour, freeing attention for much more grave problems rather than dulling it. Third, data leakage is not an inherent property of tools such as AI, but a research-design failure, as pseudonymisation and anonymisation remain the researcher’s own ethical responsibility. And lastly, AI is not Alzheimer’s for human creativity. Better tools have never suppressed creativity. They have always redirected creativity.
Now, once these arguments are set aside, what remains is not a principled position but a familiar social reflex. The one that promotes “I have suffered through this, so you should too.” It reflects in professors’ posts on LinkedIn that they won’t read a draft touched by AI. Sounds similar to one of patriarchy’s oldest tricks: the mother-in-law who insists her daughter-in-law endure what she endured, or my office clerk who advised me to pile work on a new hire, stating why should they get an easy run when we did not. Schadenfreude dressed as rigour, a bizarre satisfaction taken in someone else’s hardship. Moreover, it is not a coincidence that the loudest objections tend to belong to those who have already cleared the language-proficiency bar the rest of the world is still trying to reach.
To conclude, AI writing is a redistribution of who gets these standards, rather than the erosion of standards. The only practical choice left is whether to accept that now, or to keep resisting a novelty to be accepted at a later stage, like everyone before it. It is inevitable that it will become the new normal, and failing to see that is not caution, but a failure of foresight. In the words of historian E.H. Carr, history can only be written by those who have a sense of direction and an instinct that they are advancing towards an end goal in order to piece evidence together convincingly. And man moves within history himself and indeed progresses.
Amit Kumar is an Assistant Professor in the Institute for Development and Communication, Chandigarh

title: Letters to The Editor — August 28, 2026
content_html:
A Himalayan disaster

Two major factors behind the Nepal disaster are its mountainous terrain and the intensity of the cloudburst or the melting of glaciers in the higher Himalayan ranges. The steep slopes would have allowed gushing water to reach the plains quickly; they can also become death traps for those caught in sudden downstream flows. While the media is still trying to assess the toll, it is certain to run into the thousands. This particular disaster is unprecedented in the scale of its destruction, with hundreds of villages and small towns wiped out. It is truly heartbreaking.

V. Lakshmanan,

Tirupur, Tamil Nadu

Post-disaster relief is no longer enough. It is most essential that Himalayan nations must collaborate on joint early-warning networks, real-time data sharing, and resilient infrastructure.

Kshirasagara Balaji Rao,

Hyderabad

Revive cultural institution

Tamil Nadu’s apex cultural body, the Eyal Isai Nataka Mandram, is inactive, while the Kalaimamani State awards remain suspended. The TVK government should revive the institution, reconstitute its executive/general councils, and reform the awards process by separating classical arts from cinema.

V.P. Dhananjayan,

Chennai

title: Why 543 should remain 543
author: S.Y. Quraishi
content_html:
Days after both Houses of Parliament were adjourned sine die on August 13, 2026, the monsoon session has yet to be formally prorogued. The delay has prompted speculation that Parliament could be reconvened for another attempt at the constitutional amendment linked to delimitation and women’s reservation. Whether or not that happens, it gives urgency to a question Parliament must confront: must delimitation necessarily mean an enlargement of the Lok Sabha?

At first glance, the issue looks like arithmetic. India’s population has grown enormously since Lok Sabha seats were frozen half a century ago, so it seems natural to argue that representation must now expand correspondingly. But, constitutional design is not arithmetic alone.
